title: The Beam: how laser shows work - the planetarium years, the machines, the rules
description: An independent, cited guide to laser light shows: how a beam becomes a picture, Laserium and the planetarium era, gas tubes to diodes, how shows are programmed, why lasers can injure and who regulates them, and what a show costs.

faq.q: How does a laser show work?
faq.a: A laser beam is steered by two small mirrors on galvanometers, fast enough that the moving dot looks like solid lines and shapes. Software or a live operator decides where the dot goes, and haze in the air makes the beam visible.

faq.q: Why can you only see laser beams in fog or haze?
faq.a: A laser beam travels in one direction, so none of its light reaches your eye from the side unless something scatters it. Haze or fog particles do that scattering.

faq.q: Are laser shows safe to watch?
faq.a: Shows are designed so that any beam a person could meet stays under the exposure limit for a quarter-second accidental exposure, about 2.5 mW/cm2 for visible light. Documented audience injuries are rare; the guide's safety section covers the ones on record.

faq.q: Do you need a license to run a laser show?
faq.a: In the United States, a show laser above 5 mW of visible output needs a variance from the FDA, and outdoor beams involve the FAA. Most other countries have no specific laser show license and apply general safety law and exposure limits.

faq.q: When was the first planetarium laser show?
faq.a: Ivan Dryer's Laserium opened at Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles on November 19, 1973, performed live by an operator to recorded music.

faq.q: What was the Phoebe Bridgers planetarium laser show?
faq.a: Phoebe Bridgers previewed her album Lost Weekend in 44 planetariums from August 10 to 14, 2026, with either a fulldome show or a laser show designed by Laser Fantasy.
